problems.title: Problem 9.6(a) original
problems.source: Original Chapter9 Problems9.6–9.9 in user-uploaded excerpt
problems.prompt:
Consider again the facts of Problem 9.4 under each variation presented. Which constitute constructive fraud under the UFTA and UVTA? Those facts are:

a. Debtor owes 10 creditors $50,000, and is in default on 7 of the debts. Five creditors bring lawsuits against the Debtor. Debtor's only nonexempt asset is a valuable painting she inherited from her father, worth $40,000. Debtor sells the painting to Art Mann, a wealthy collector, for $38,000. Art Mann knows nothing of Debtor's financial situation. Debtor deposits the cash in her bank, wire transfers the money to a Swiss bank, and disappears. Two months later, an involuntary chapter 7 order for relief is entered against Debtor.

problems.title: Problem 9.7 original guarantee
problems.source: Original Chapter9 Problems9.6–9.9 in user-uploaded excerpt
problems.prompt: Boering Corp. is a manufacturer of jet aircrafts whose primary customer is Deltoid Airlines. Deltoid began experiencing severe financial difficulties and, eventually, fuel suppliers refused to sell Deltoid any more fuel on credit. In order to keep Deltoid flying, Boering agreed with Deltoid's fuel suppliers to guarantee repayment for any future fuel shipments to Deltoid on ordinary credit terms. Deltoid's financial problems were beyond repair, though, and Deltoid ceased operations three months later, at which time Deltoid owed fuel suppliers $6 million for purchases guaranteed by Boering. Deltoid's demise and Boering's consequent customer loss and guaranty liability also strained the financial resources of Boering, who filed a chapter 11 petition six months after Deltoid ceased operations. Boering, as chapter 11 debtor in possession, has brought an action to avoid its guaranty of Deltoid's fuel purchases as constructively fraudulent. How should the court rule?

problems.title: Problem 9.8(a) original
problems.source: Original Chapter9 Problems9.6–9.9 in user-uploaded excerpt
problems.prompt:
Amelia Alpha and O.J. Omega were top executives of Target Corp., a medical supply firm. Target Corp. had no secured debt, $15 million in unsecured debt, and assets estimated at $23 million, leaving equity of $8 million. Alpha and Omega decided to buy out Target and take it private, believing that the company would make huge profits if it refocused its business on cloning. Alpha and Omega agreed to buy all of the existing stock for $8 million, putting up $500,000 of their own money and borrowing $7.5 million from Lender. They also gave Lender a security interest in all of Target's assets, and had Target guarantee payment of the $7.5 million debt. The old stockholders were cashed out for $8 million, and Alpha and Omega took control of Target. After this transaction — a “leveraged buyout” (LBO) — Target had total debt of $22.5 million ($15 million unsecured plus $7.5 million secured) and assets estimated to be worth $23 million, leaving equity of at most $500,000.

The next year cloning was outlawed by treaty. Target went bankrupt. The trustee challenged the LBO as a fraudulent transfer, and sought (1) to avoid Lender's security interest in Target's assets, and (2) to recover the money paid to the original stockholders of Target.

a. What is the “transfer” that is potentially subject to avoidance?

problems.title: Problem 9.9(a) original
problems.source: Original Chapter9 Problems9.6–9.9 in user-uploaded excerpt
problems.prompt:
Parent has filed a chapter 7 petition. Each of the following transactions occurred within the two years before the petition date, at a time when Parent was insolvent. For each transaction, analyze whether there was a transfer made or obligation incurred that is avoidable as either actually or constructively fraudulent? If so, from whom (if anyone) can the trustee recover?

a. Parent made a gift to her adult child, Child 1, to enable Child 1 to pay Child 1's college tuition at University. Upon receipt of those funds from Parent, Child 1 paid them to University in satisfaction of Child 1's tuition obligation to University. University took those funds in good faith and without knowledge of the voidability of any transfer or obligation.
